content:
Earlier this year, I swapped out a battery-powered push mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users have to manually drive it around the perimeter of the yard once to build a virtual map. Once set up, the machine carries out mowing tasks automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be the easier choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9, which I reviewed earlier this year, is how each machine makes sense of your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses what the company calls the TerraVision 2.0 system. Three cameras allow the mower to map the lawn automatically, with no need to install boundary wires in advance or add an extra RTK antenna.

Building the initial map automatically takes longer. However, I think this method may be easier to get to grips with for users who are less tech-savvy.

To verify that, I specifically asked my mum, who lives in another state, to install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without any help from me. She replied that everything worked fine. But I am not entirely sure she would have had the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire boundary and then manually mark out the areas it should avoid.

Automatic mapping ran into a small hiccup in my front yard. There is no fence or other physical divider between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, so TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's grass in my map.

I fixed the problem by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. Still, if a lawn does not have a clear visual boundary, the initial mapping process may call for a bit of extra attention.

Watching through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to open that view in a large window. That let me work indoors while watching, from the robot's own point of view, how it navigated the back yard.

This feature is not essential for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more entertaining, and it occasionally helps to explain why it slows down or steers clear of certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps share plenty of similar design elements in other respects. Both let you schedule jobs, adjust mowing behaviour, divide zones, mark off areas to avoid, and remotely control the mower.

On that last feature, TerraMow has one particularly nice twist. As well as the usual left-right virtual sticks, its app offers a one-handed joystick mode. You hold the iPhone normally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving a mower with an iPhone is not the main point of either system. Ideally, the robot should just get on with things on its preset schedule with no intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick control is surprisingly handy for tidying up patches it missed.

At times, I almost felt like I was controlling the robot by telekinesis (that lovely sense of it). I could hold the iPhone down at my side while I walked, and with just a small thumb movement, the machine would head in my direction.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control method.

A more aggressive mower

Overall, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while working.

I would not say the TerraMow is noisy. But the difference is clear. The Anthbot can run very quietly, so quietly that it is easy to forget it is still going, even when it is mowing after sunset with headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to work reliably. That makes daytime scheduling all the more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and is bigger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow ships with a protective garage that can cover the charging dock, while the Anthbot's garage has to be bought separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently stable and reliable. I relied on it for the mowing over several weeks in a row without needing to step in myself.

When adaptive mapping gets a bit too clever

The same visual smarts that make TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower keeps updating its map based on what it sees. Saving those updates after every job takes a while, and during that time you cannot do anything else in the app.

After several days of rain in a row, I ran into an interesting edge case. Puddles appeared in parts of the yard, and the TerraMow sensibly avoided that area on its next run.

The grass inside the circular area it skipped started growing taller. As time went on, the mower seemed to treat that patch of tall grass as something it should keep avoiding, and even once the ground had dried out, that patch kept being left out of the run.

I sorted it by using the remote-control feature in the app to manually drive the mower over the tall patch and mow it. Once the area was back to a normal lawn, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow get closer to boundaries with more confidence. If the grass in an area where the boundary is unclear grows too tall, the system may treat it as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot approach feels less adaptive and depends more heavily on the boundaries and obstacles you set yourself. That method needs more upfront work, but it also avoids the map "changing its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

Having used both systems, for most people I would lean towards recommending TerraMow's camera approach.

Laying boundary wires beforehand is a complete non-starter for me, and installing an RTK base station means having another piece of hardware to position, power and maintain. TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needed a manual fix, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

All of those issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, a great live camera view, and the best manual controls I have come across in a robotic mower app.

I genuinely enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. Handing that job over to a robot gives me more time to spend on landscaping, edging and the detail work while keeping the lawn looking tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 has performed well enough for me to recommend it, especially for anyone who wants robotic mowing without the hassle of burying wire, installing an RTK antenna, or having to walk the iPhone around the whole yard by hand.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999, available on the site with a $200 coupon. You can also find the product on TerraMow's official website.
